extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers interested in philosophical and psychological theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of major philosophical and psychological theories about laughter and humor, their historical proponents, mechanisms, examples, critiques, and the cultural/ethical roles of comedy. Useful as a reference for understanding competing accounts of what makes things funny and what functions humor serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Our laughter expresses feelings of superiority over other people or over a former state of ourselves; laughter often involves scorn or malicious delight in another's self-ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with Plato, Hobbes, Descartes, and later proponents (e.g., Roger Scruton). Examples include laughing at someone's perceived defects or misfortunes. Criticisms: Hutcheson, Chaplin examples, and others show cases where feelings of superiority are neither necessary nor sufficient for laughter (e.g., self-directed laughter, admiration of skill). Historical implications: used to condemn laughter as morally objectionable and to restrict comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter releases pent-up nervous or psychic energy — a discharge analogous to a pressure valve releasing built-up energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versions traced from Shaftesbury to Spencer, Dewey, and Freud: Shaftesbury's animal spirits, Spencer's nervous energy discharged in non-purposeful muscular action, Dewey's relaxation of strain, Freud's release of energy summoned to repress feelings or to think. Examples: jokes that make prior pity superfluous; Harry Graham's poem, Mark Twain story. Criticisms: hydraulic physiology is outdated; Freud's specific psychoanalytic claims (repressed sexuality/hostility as primary) and mimetic representation are questioned by evidence and conceptual problems; contemporary scholars seldom accept Relief Theory as a general explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from the perception of something incongruous—something that violates our mental patterns and expectations; laughter follows the sudden transformation or dissipation of a strained expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed by philosophers such as Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard. Practical form: the set-up creates an expectation and the punch violates it (set-up/punch structure). Kant emphasizes the sudden transformation of strained expectation into nothing; Schopenhauer locates incongruity between perception and abstract concepts. Variants differ on whether mere incongruity suffices or whether resolution is required (see two-stage models). Examples: wordplay, unexpected endings, absurd juxtapositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and Punch (joke structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke typically has a set-up that creates an expectation and a punch (line) that violates that expectation; the punch's violation of expectation produces the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structure is ancient (Aristotle, Cicero) and underlies much stand-up technique. Effective jokes use the set-up to guide the audience's interpretation and the punch to redirect it. Repeating a joke can reduce the surprise but may still be funny if reinterpretation occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage / Resolution Model (Schultz & Suls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor appreciation involves two stages: detection of an incongruity and the subsequent cognitive resolution (fitting the anomalous element into a conceptual schema); enjoyment comes from resolving incongruity rather than incongruity alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schultz argues that after about age seven we require fitting of the anomaly; unresolved incongruity is classified as 'nonsense' rather than humor. This model explains 'getting' a joke and differentiates funny incongruity from mere confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freud's Three Laughter Situations (der Witz, the comic, humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud distinguishes three kinds of laughter situations: der Witz (jokes/witty remarks) where released energy is that used to repress feelings; the comic, where released energy is the energy of thinking used to understand a movement; and humor, where psychic energy summoned for feeling becomes superfluous and is released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud connects joke content to repressed sexual/hostile material and theorizes mechanisms like mimetic representation. The entry presents Freud's examples and also notes major criticisms: many of Freud's claims are questionable or empirically unsupported; joke creation can be conscious and his energy-account mechanisms are problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as Play / Laughter as Play Signal (Play Theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter evolved from mock-aggressive play in apes; laughter functions as a play signal that coordinates non-serious interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evolutionary account links human humor to primate play fighting and suggests benefits such as social bonding and safe simulation of aggression. It helps address traditional objections by framing humor as a form of play with attendant cognitive and social benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs. Tragedy: Characteristic Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy embodies an anti-heroic, pragmatic attitude, valuing cleverness, adaptability, common speech, and group/family as units; tragedy emphasizes heroic idealism, elevated language, and singular great individuals (kings, generals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aristophanes, Chaplin, Michael Moore for comedy; tragic heroes valorize Warrior Virtues. Comedy's methods include deal-making, trickery, escape; it often features more prominent roles for women and lower-class protagonists. These genre features explain comedy's social functions (anti-elitist, inclusive) and moral/political stances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits / Functions of Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor yields psychological and physical health benefits, fosters mental flexibility, serves as a social lubricant, and can encourage critical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry notes empirical findings supporting these benefits and argues that comedy's features align with philosophic practices (e.g., critical reflection, attention to language), suggesting positive civic and cognitive roles for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as Conceptual Skill (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit consists in the ability to find for an object a conception under which it can be thought though it differs greatly from other objects under that conception; humor arises when one perceives the incongruity between concept and perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include concise intellectual jokes that exploit category mismatches. This criterion treats clever conceptual reclassification as a source of amusement and as a mental skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and Social Objections to Laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can be morally objectionable when it expresses malice, overthrows rational self-control, or is associated with idleness, lust, or hostility; authorities (Plato, Stoics, Christian ascetics) argued for restraint or suppression of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical prescriptions include limiting comedic representation to lower-status performers or forbidding loud/unrestrained laughter. The entry documents these critiques and their influence on cultural attitudes toward humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as Insult / Offense (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being laughed at is offensive because laughter asserts a profound incongruity between the laughed-at person's conceptions and reality; the laugh of scorn publicly announces the other's conceptual failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion explains why certain forms of laughter (scornful laughter) are psychologically painful and socially injurious; it distinguishes benign amusement from humiliating mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/Skill-based Humor (Physical Comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some humor arises from admiration of surprising physical skill or clever escapes (e.g., Chaplin, Keaton) rather than feelings of superiority over the comic's misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in silent film where heroes perform acrobatic feats to escape danger produce laughter without invoking superiority. This undermines simple superiority accounts and supports alternative theories (incongruity, appreciation of skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary Accounts: Sexual Selection / Signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor production and appreciation can function as sexually selected traits or honest signals of intelligence, creativity, or social value in mate selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited work includes Bressler, Martin, Greengross, and others who treat humor as a trait favored in sexual selection or mate choice. The entry surveys competing evolutionary proposals and empirical studies linking humor to desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption / Knowledge-based Signaling Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Encryption Theory suggests humor is a knowledge-based mechanism for honest signaling: comedic content encodes information accessible only to those who share certain knowledge, thereby signaling group membership or intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced work (Flamson & Barrett) treats humor as a way to transmit and verify shared knowledge; this explains crossword-like or culturally-specific jokes that exclude outsiders while rewarding insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Incongruity and Nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all incongruity counts as humor; unresolvable incongruity that cannot be cognitively reconciled is 'nonsense' rather than humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction (emphasized by Schultz and others) serves as a diagnostic: if the audience cannot reinterpret the set-up to accommodate the punch, the effect is confusion, not amusement. Age and cognitive development affect whether resolution is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinities Between Standup Comedy and Philosophy (criteria for philosophically effective comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standup comedy and philosophy share features: conversational form, reflection on familiar puzzling experiences, questioning stance, emotional disengagement, critical thinking, attention to language, and a pleasure in surprising thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven affinities function as criteria for standup that resonates philosophically: routines that prompt reflective surprise, linguistic precision, and critical challenge resemble philosophical practice and can deliver intellectual as well as comic pleasure.
